LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

Industry observers note that as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

It has been revealed that while you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an key investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she states. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.).

Sources indicate that but, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s important to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most key factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Sources indicate that hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

Recent findings suggest that the Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz says her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

The Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

These shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

In a recent development, read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro.

In a recent development, on has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It has been revealed that it’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

Sources indicate that this sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

Recent findings suggest that while there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best On Walking Shoes.

According to recent reports, think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

The Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

This sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an concern. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

The best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

This isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait problems as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

The Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t plan to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

Recent findings suggest that it's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

Industry observers note that there’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Sources indicate that like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

There’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

The level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

Long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

It has been revealed that the Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

The Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

Industry observers note that the right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The New Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

Let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

Sources indicate that this shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis.

The lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

Sources indicate that the heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

Recent findings suggest that these shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

Read More: Best lululemon Shoes Ranked.

There’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

Sources indicate that this shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.).

Sources indicate that asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

It has been revealed that the best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

The Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

Sources indicate that the Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.).

It has been revealed that maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

In a recent development, medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

Sources indicate that this is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

In a recent development, this is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

In a recent development, running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” notes Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”.

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:.

According to recent reports, toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially key during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Recent findings suggest that length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

It has been revealed that arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no issues wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

Sources indicate that the type of running workouts you initiative to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

A stability shoe can help correct gait complications like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is important for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

According to recent reports, you should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a latest pair.

Sources indicate that running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

Sources indicate that A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” claims Jess Cooney.
  • It has been revealed that cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea.
  • According to recent reports, cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” claims Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

It has been revealed that cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in Newly introduced York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney.

According to recent reports, cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

“We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

Sources indicate that the husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” claims the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it.

In a recent development, cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” says Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s Latest White.

The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” claims Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”.

It has been revealed that the architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

To expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” indicates Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Sources indicate that cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

With a view over the living room, Cooney says the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

Industry observers note that the clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” indicates the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

“I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” claims Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” states Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

The view overlooking the Berkshires.

Latest Update: Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

Industry observers note that “Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

It has been revealed that participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based problems like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

Industry observers note that “Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

Sources indicate that sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, stated that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

Sources indicate that “Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

In a recent development, “There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she stated. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” stated that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall remarked.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie revealed the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

It has been revealed that “We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” claims Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

In a recent development, “Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” stated Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The tech giant says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that FINDING THE PERFECT gym shorts shouldn’t feel harder than your workout. You know the struggle—shorts that ride up, cling in all the wrong places, or leave you chafed before you’ve even finished your warm-up. Truth is, you and those hard-earned leg muscles deserve better. Way better.

Sources indicate that whether you’re a gym veteran who can’t stop talking about leg day or a newbie figuring out the difference between a dumbbell and a kettlebell, it’s time to upgrade. According to Michael Hamlin, NSCA, CSCS, your athletic shorts should "allow you to perform basic workouts without too much hassle," from treadmill intervals to back squatting in the gym. Translation: You need shorts that stay put, don’t bunch up, and definitely don’t shout, "I just rolled out of bed.".

So, we did the work for you—literally. We tested a whole locker’s worth of gym shorts, got insights from fitness pros, influencers, and even the designers behind them, and narrowed it down to the best six pairs for you. The right gym shorts should enhance, not hinder, your workout—just like the best workout shirts, the best joggers, and the best workout clothes in general. They should fit securely, wick sweat effectively, and allow full mobility for any exercise. The best gym shorts will have you feeling like a gym rock star, looking like you stepped off the cover of a fitness mag, and—most importantly—keeping your thighs cool and your glutes wedgie-free. Now that’s worth showing off.

The Ten Thousand Interval Short with Liner is the gritty MVP of gym shorts—versatile, durable, and ready for anything. Loved by athletes and editors alike, we use the Interval Short for everything from grueling lifting sessions to intense conditioning work to cooldown and recovery.

Men’s Health Senior Editor Brett Williams, NASM, is also a fan: "These are my go-to for just about every activity, from strength workouts to walking the dog. The fit, stretchy-yet-solid materials, and bountiful pockets stand out above the other shorts in my drawer.".

Available in lined or unlined versions and three inseam lengths, the Interval Short checks every box. Its four-way stretch fabric offers a full range of motion, quick-drying capabilities, and an athletic fit that feels snug but breathable. Whether you’re crushing a WOD, running sprints, or chilling in the sauna, these shorts can handle it.

For years, Rhone has been cranking out workout gear so good it’ll make you wonder why you ever settled for anything less. The Pursuit Short takes things to the next level, building on the success of Rhone's Mako Short. Thanks to a durable polyester-spandex blend, these shorts give you enough stretch to handle everything from Netflix marathons on the couch to actual marathons on the pavement.

With three inseam lengths (5", 7", and 9") and the choice of lined or unlined, there’s a pair for every activity and every guy. Need support for leg day? Go lined. Prefer a lighter feel for a casual jog or coffee run? Unlined has you covered. The stretch fabric moves with you without giving up on durability. And the zippered pockets? Game-changer. No more chasing your phone mid-burpee.

Whether you’re crushing your workout or just crushing avocado toast, the Pursuit Short does it all—and looks great doing it.

Read More: What Is Moisture-Wicking?

Industry observers note that the Vuori Kore Short is a great multitasker—soft, stretchy, and ready to handle whatever your day throws at you. Made with a blend of recycled polyester and elastane, they’re eco-friendly and feel like a dream. Plus, the built-in boxer-brief liner keeps you supported and sweat-free, so you can focus on your workout instead of readjusting your twig and berries every five seconds.

With 5", 7", and 9" inseam options, there’s a fit for everyone, whether you’re squatting, stretching, or just sitting on the couch pretending you worked out. Two hand pockets and a back pocket are great for storage, but let’s be real—if you’re carrying your keys while running, you’re playing with fire.

Now, the price—$78. Yeah, it’s an investment. But you’re getting shorts that look good at the gym and the smoothie bar afterward. These shorts are so versatile, you can smash your workout, then crash on the couch—because let’s be honest, they double as comfy pajamas.

According to recent reports, the Lululemon Pace Breaker Linerless Short might just be the unicorn of gym shorts—lightweight, comfortable, and fresh even after the sweatiest leg day. After two years of putting them through the wringer, I’m still amazed by how cool they feel mid-workout and how they bounce back like nothing happened. Credit Lululemon’s brilliant design: no liner, four-way stretch that moves with you, and a back mesh panel that’s basically AC for your glutes. Redesigned low-bounce hand pockets and a zippered compartment keep essentials secure, so you’re not scrambling for your locker key mid-burpee.

"I’ve run dozens of miles wearing this short," states Senior Editor Brett Williams. They’re made of super light material, but the waistband’s fit is solid. The pockets aren’t too deep, and a zipper compartment is perfect for storing keys on the go.

Bottom line: These shorts make you feel like you’re gliding through your workout—and they’ve got enough stretch to handle those extra post-workout tacos, too.

According to recent reports, the Nike Form Men’s Dri-FIT 7" Unlined Versatile Shorts are basically the Swiss Army knife of gym shorts—flexible, comfy, and sustainable to boot. They offer an unbeatable combination of comfort and flexibility, making them perfect for everything from jogging to lifting weights. You’ll like how these shorts will keep up with your workout without turning you into a sweaty mess.

Sources indicate that thanks to Nike’s Dri-FIT technology, they wick sweat faster than you can say "leg day." The unlined design is so lightweight and free-moving, you might forget you’re wearing them (don’t worry, they’re still on). Unlined, lightweight, moisture-wicking, and the capacity for complete freedom of movement—that’s exactly what you need in great gym shorts, and these deliver on that.

The 7-inch inseam is perfect for squats, lunges, or making a fashion statement without looking like you borrowed your dad’s basketball shorts. Bonus? They’re made from sustainable materials, so you can feel good about saving the planet while crushing PRs. At just $35, these shorts do it all without breaking the bank—or your stride.

In a recent development, the Alo Circuit Short blends comfort, style, and performance so effortlessly you might forget you’re wearing them—don’t worry, you are. With a minimal, relaxed fit and a stretchy drawstring waist, these shorts are as comfortable as they are functional. The 7-inch inseam hits the sweet spot—enough coverage for confidence, but still letting your legs breathe.

Industry observers note that and let’s talk about those deep zippered side pockets—they’ve got room for your phone, keys, and wallet without anything flying out mid-jumping jack. The fabric? It’s that happy blend of 86 percent polyester and 14 percent elastane, softly swishy and sweat-wicking to keep you cool, even if the guy next to you in spin class is not.

Industry observers note that sizing is true to fit, with inseams ranging from 5 inches for size small to 7 inches for 2XL. At $68, they’re not the cheapest, but they’re versatile enough to justify it. Throw on a hoodie, and you’re smoothie-bar ready. Functional, stylish, and just flashy enough to make you the coolest guy in the gym—just don’t get caught doing arm curls in the squat rack.

Recent findings suggest that skip the cotton—it’s a sweat sponge. Synthetic fabrics like polyester blends are moisture-wicking and dry promptly, while nylon blends are more breathable for hot weather. Look for spandex or elastane for that four-way stretch, so you can move freely without restriction. Bonus: Some materials, like merino wool, are naturally anti-stink, while others feature built-in odor-fighting technology to keep you smelling fresh, no matter how hard you go.

Sources indicate that lined shorts offer built-in support, making them ideal for high-impact activities. "Unlined shorts offer more versatility for layering, while lined shorts provide additional support and comfort for high-impact activities," says Hamlin. If you’re lifting heavy or going ape on the air bike, the liner is a win. For casual workouts or layering over tights, unlined shorts let you move freely and stay cool.

The inseam is the length of the shorts from your nether region to the inside hem, and getting it right can make or break your workout. If you’re doing moves like squats, lunges, or anything that’s got you moving deep and low, shorter inseams (think 5 to 7 inches) are your best bet for keeping things smooth and unrestricted. While shorter inseams offer better mobility, longer inseams of 9 to 11 inches are great for taller athletes or anyone who wants extra coverage. Just keep in mind, if you’re on the shorter side, too much fabric can feel bulky and might even slow you down.

Functional storage is a must. "I say pockets are a must for me, and an extra bonus if they zip. Not a pocket in the back of my waist that I can barely reach, but pockets on the front sides," notes Andy Stern from Rumble Boxing. Side pockets keep your essentials handy, and zippers keep you from chasing keys mid-jog.

Recent findings suggest that your gym shorts should feel as good as they look. Elastic waistbands with drawstrings keep you secure, while lightweight, breathable fabrics keep you comfortable and focused. Gym shorts should fit snugly around your waist—no squeezing, no sliding down mid-squat. Think "secure but free to move," like your gym buddy who knows when to spot you and when to back off. If you’re lunging and your shorts are riding up, it’s time to re-evaluate.

It has been revealed that when it comes to picking gym shorts, it’s all about matching your moves. If you’re running, go for shorter inseams and split hems—you want freedom of movement, not fabric flapping around like you’re in a wind tunnel. Plus, reflective details keep you visible, because dodging traffic shouldn’t be part of your cardio. For lifting, you’ll need durable fabrics and compression liners to keep everything secure while you chase your personal best—nobody needs a wardrobe malfunction mid-squat. And for yoga? Think soft, stretchy, and unlined, so you can nail that downward dog without feeling like your shorts are plotting against you.

Flattering shorts come down to fit, proportion, and the right inseam for your build. If you’ve got beefy legs, short shorts will always work in your favor. Show them off with a 5-inch inseam (or less), which hits mid-thigh for most guys. For a touch more coverage, go with a 7-inch inseam, the most popular length for a casual, everyday look. Aim for a slight taper through the leg so it holds its shape without clinging. Bonus points for a smooth waistband that won’t dig in.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to try and test all kinds of gym shorts. I also enlisted help from our team of style and fitness editors, including members of our Men's Health advisory board. For months, we personally tested dozens of workout shorts. These weren’t casual try-ons; we put them through their paces in real training sessions.

Our evaluation focused on four key areas: comfort, performance (think moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and breathability), type (lined or unlined), and durability. Comfort and functionality are non-negotiable, especially for guys tackling intense training. Our mission? To find gym shorts that not only look great but also withstand tough workouts and the test of time.

In a recent development, we weren’t interested in trendy or fad-driven designs. Instead, we prioritized gym shorts that work for athletic guys who train hard, offer exceptional value at reasonable price points, and maintain a timeless style. The result? A curated list of six gym shorts that feel great, perform even better, and will look sharp for years to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.

According to recent reports, I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises. While recent research suggests that weighted vests may not have a dramatic impact on bone density, they’re still a safe and convenient way to increase the load on your muscles and joints, helping you push yourself a little harder than usual.

Industry observers note that weighted vests let you add extra resistance to walking, stair climbing, jumping, push-ups, and pull-ups without needing to grip dumbbells or barbells. Some clients even wear them during everyday activities like cleaning, yard work, or mowing the lawn—making fitness a little more functional and, yes, a bit more fun.

That noted, if you’ve been diagnosed with osteoporosis, consult your doctor before adding a weighted vest to your exercise routine, while folks who are pregnant or experience back, neck, or joint pain should also avoid them.

Industry observers note that before you take the plunge on purchasing a weighted vest, you should consider the resistance level, workouts such as walking or HIIT, and whether materials are sweat-resistant to determine which one is best for you. Ready to get vested?

After testing a handful of weighted vests for weeks, the trophy goes to the Omorpho G-Vest for its remarkable comfort, ideal weight, and sleek design. I spent a week wearing it for my regular lifting sessions and hour-long walks. It’s easy to wear for my normal gym routine, which includes moves such as walking lunges, Copenhagen planks, pull-ups, and push-ups.

According to recent reports, however, I found it to be challenging when worn for heavier compound lifts like front squats, deadlifts, and barbell rows. Other than walking lunges, I wouldn’t normally add load to those exercises because of the logistics of holding or hanging weight, but the vest makes it possible to add resistance without gripping anything.

Industry observers note that the fit is another reason the G-Vest earns the top spot. This vest is surprisingly comfortable considering it weighs just over five pounds from stainless steel balls. While the back panels have more weight—226 stainless steel balls on the back and 122 on the front—the weight distribution feels uniform when wearing.

In a recent development, it’s also compact—from the shoulder straps to the bottom of the vest is about 17 inches, which, for me, is great since I have a very short torso. It also doesn't dig into the top of my hip bone when I move around.

Industry observers note that even if you don’t have a short torso, you’ll still appreciate the soft-to-the-touch polyester fabric, despite it feeling like neoprene (synthetic rubber). I use adjustable cords at the sides for a customized fit. There are also straps on the shoulders to accommodate a wider frame, or if you want the vest to sit a little lower on your torso. For reference, I have mine on the shortest setting.

Recent findings suggest that one downside of the G-Vest is its limited size options. There are only two: S/M or L/XL. I highly recommend using the size chart to determine which fit is best for you. I’m typically a medium when shopping for athletic tops, but I chose the L/XL because my chest circumference is on the cusp of both options. It’s also worth mentioning that the weight of the S/M vest is four pounds and 12 ounces, while the L/XL is five pounds and six ounces.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Review.

Sources indicate that you can shell out up to $300 for a weighted vest, but not everyone needs all the extra features that come with that higher price tag. The ApexUp weighted vest is a popular option thanks to its low price point, but it offers more than just savings.

This vest is built from neoprene (which is the durable synthetic rubber you’ll find in wetsuits) and filled with iron sand, a material that’s denser than natural sand and absorbs less moisture. As a result, it won’t stick to you or clump up when you sweat.

In a recent development, it has a smooth, comfortable feel, with seams that are stitched over with fabric to prevent rubbing and chafing. Wide armholes and an adjustable strap across the chest mean you can get a comfortable fit, no matter your chest size.

Sources indicate that the solo strap in ApexUp’s 10-pound version means it’s more likely to shift around during dynamic movements like burpees, making this vest a better choice for things like walking. A lot of the weight in the vest is in the front straps, so just be aware of your posture while you use this. But the mesh storage pocket in back is secure and roomy enough for your phone, which is a nice feature if you want to free up your hands.

A common complaint with this vest is the smell, which may be due to that neoprene cover. If you notice it and it bothers you, just let the vest air out a little before using it. Also, be aware that the ApexUp vest doesn’t allow you to tack on extra weight. But at this low price, you can simply buy a upcoming one when you’re ready for more resistance and still come out on top, price-wise.

In a recent development, the best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

According to recent reports, one way WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT likes to use weighted vests in her own training and with her training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement.

The Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. Grief tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around her apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional clothing layer than a traditional weighted vest.

The aluminum front buckles feel sturdy. The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once Grief found the right adjustment, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation, and the straps stayed put. “I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

Read More: Stakt Weighted Vest Review.

If you’re looking for an adjustable-weight option ideal for specific functional training exercises and rucking, the Hyper Vest Elite from Hyperwear is highly customizable. I tested the 10-pound model, which is weighted with 66 individual 2.25-ounce stainless steel bars, each with its own little pocket.

If you prefer heavier weights, 15- and 20-pound options are available. Plus, you can purchase a box of individual weights to load up your vest (each pocket can fit two 2.25-ounce weights).

Industry observers note that I wore it during multiple 60-minute walks, squats, pull-ups, push-ups, and back extensions. With the full 10 pounds loaded on my body, I found it really difficult to do pull-ups and push-ups. However, when I removed some of the weights from the individual pockets, it made for a more manageable load.

In a recent development, that stated, I’m not sure how realistic it is to load up these tiny weights into individual pouches when switching between exercises. I think it’s a great feature, but personally, I’d design my workouts to ensure I didn’t have to adjust the weights more than once.

There are adjustable cords on each side to cinch or loosen for your preferred fit, but you won’t find shoulder strap adjustments like on the Omorpho vests. I also noticed the Hyperwear vest sits nearly five inches lower on my torso than the Omorpho vest. It doesn’t dig into my hips, but I notice it grazes my lower back when walking. It’s not a deal breaker, but I prefer shorter styles. Four size options are available: small, medium, large, and extra large.

As for material, I appreciate the heavy-duty construction of this vest, which is made with Cordura, a synthetic, tear-resistant fabric popular for backpacks and military clothing. It will hold up for years, even if you plan to go hiking or wear it in the elements. I also like the reflective strips at the zipper and across the chest for increased visibility outdoors.

If you’re looking for a weighted vest with resistance that pushes your limits while not disrupting your range of motion, this one by Vivitory checks the box. Despite the non-cropped fit, it still stays in place with only two adjustable straps and distributes weight evenly (11 pounds for the medium size and 18 pounds for the large size).

Industry observers note that WH art director Christine Giordano was pleasantly surprised by how light it felt compared to holding it. “I was nervous it was going to be too heavy for me or cause pain in my lower back, but I was wrong,” claims Giordano. “It didn’t bounce up and down or move all over—it stayed snug to my body while not being too hot and bulky.”.

It has been revealed that she loves wearing it during easy walks when waiting around for her kids’ sporting events or for more intense workouts, such as CrossFit or burpees. “I’m not a huge fan of dumbbell step-ups, so I tried it with the vest for the added weight without leaning forward,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that as for the material, it’s made with neoprene, a synthetic rubber resistant to sweat that Giordano says she found to be breathable. There are also reflective strips on the vest for visibility during dawn or dusk, and a small pouch at the back for holding essentials.

In a recent development, if you get seriously sweaty during cardio or weightlifting, this 12-pound Reebok weighted vest is an option in hot summer temps. The back has a breathable ventilation panel that allows air to circulate.

WH contributor Korin Miller has recently added it to her workout gear lineup. “I like to go hard with my workouts, and I get really sweaty as a result—I appreciate the open-air design of this vest so I can cool off,” indicates Miller. “That, combined with the airy fabric, means I won’t end up with the vest sticking against my skin during workouts.”.

Recent findings suggest that aside from its sweat-wicking properties, its two adjustable straps allow for a customized fit during a variety of workouts. For Miller, specifically walking, cycling, rowing, and bodyweight movements, such as planks and squats.

According to recent reports, but, it’s vital to note this model isn’t ideal for jumping. “Those extra weights can flap around during bigger movements like running and HIIT workouts—basically anything that has you jumping up and down,” claims Miller.

Read More: Reebok Weighted Vest Review.

The Omorpho G-Vest Icon is a quality choice for runners and HIIT workouts, given its snug fit and moderate weight that doesn’t feel like too much. The design is really similar to Omorpho’s OG model, with soft neoprene-style fabric, stainless steel ball bearings embedded into the fabric, and waist and shoulder adjustments for a custom fit.

The main difference is the adjustable weight and reflective strips throughout for extra visibility during night runs. The adjustable weight system is genius. It involves “G-Packs” of varying weights that snap in and out, allowing you to tack on additional, evenly distributed weight fast. (Just a heads up: A set of three G-Packs that brings the weight up to 12 pounds costs an extra $129.).

We also like that the encased stainless steel weights are not featured through the chest area. If you want to wear the G-Vest Icon with just a sports bra, you won’t have any irritation from high-impact movements.

For reference, the weights go up the entirety of the front panels on the men’s version. While the vest’s fitted style is ideal for runs, its six-pound weight means it’s better suited for things like short runs and sprints.

One downside is that the neoprene-style fabric made our tester sweat a ton when worn with layers. “My first experience with the vest was under my winter jacket on a 10-degree day during an hour-long walk,” WH contributor Korin Miller indicates. “I sweat my butt off despite the cold temperatures, compared to having sweat evaporate from my skin at the gym.”.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Icon Review.

Besides being a WH Fitness Awards 2025 winner, the Empower Weighted Vest is the only vest we’ve seen with a cross-style fit. It’s designed specifically to fit women’s curves while offering supreme support for the shoulder blades. The fit is compact with less material at the sides, while the straps are fully adjustable.

Sources indicate that while its main highlight is being a custom fit for women, another unique feature is six removable one-pound bags (three in the front and three in the back pockets). In the 10-pound model (weight ranges from eight to 16 pounds), the vest can go as low as four pounds when the weights are removed if you’re seeking only light resistance.

It has been revealed that WH health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, uses it for taking her workouts to the next level. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” she notes. Her only complaint is that the removable weights can make it feel bulky and interfere with hitting the full range of motion with a handful of exercises. “If I wanted to do crunches, I couldn’t lie on my back without it arching, and I couldn’t do supermans from my stomach because the bags in the front made it so I couldn’t lie flat,” she says. “During other strength exercises like squats, it hit the top of my thigh and prevented me from moving down further.” Perhaps it’s best to use the added pocket weights only during walks.

As for material, it’s neoprene for optimal sweat resistance, like the Vivitory and Prodigen weighted vests.

Not everyone wants or needs the 20-pound resistance TRX’s Hexgrip Weighted Vest can offer. But this vest is adjustable, allowing you to tweak the weight in one-pound increments, giving you room to grow up to that 20 pounds. So, if you want to use it as a 10-pound vest to start, more power to you.

This sturdy vest helps you get a secure fit with the help of three wide Velcro straps, making it a solid option for dynamic movements, some cardio workouts, and general strength training. The neoprene inner is comfortable against your skin, while the snug fit and smartly positioned weights mean you don’t have to stress about the vest moving around on you while you work out.

While it’s on the heavier end, it’s not bulky. As a result, you can still feel comfortable doing your usual range of motion. Just a heads up: Some of the weights are positioned across the chest, which may feel more noticeable if you have larger breasts. But those adjustable straps mean you can lower or raise the shoulder straps to find a position that’s more comfortable for you.

In a recent development, the weights slip into individual pockets to prevent them from shifting around, but make sure they’re secured well before you start your workout. (Some people have reported them sliding out.) Because the adjustment process takes some time, this isn’t a vest you’ll want to adjust mid-workout. This vest also comes in a 40-pound version, although most exercisers will do best with the 20-pounder as a heavy option.

Sources indicate that if you have broader shoulders, the RITFIT has fully adjustable straps. They're spaced further apart—one sits higher on your chest and the other closer to your waist.

It can be more comfortable if you have a larger chest, while it may run bigger on smaller frames. It also has mesh pockets to store your keys and phone.

According to recent reports, the load on a weighted vest can range from 3 to over 30 pounds, depending on the style and brand. If you’ve never used a weighted vest or are new to resistance training, I recommend starting with a lighter option between 3 and 10 pounds. Our best overall pick is optimal for newbies since it’s five pounds.

It has been revealed that heavier vests are ideal for loading bodyweight exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, squats, and walking lunges. They can also be used for walking, hiking, or rucking, depending on your fitness level. Lighter vests are ideal for speed training like sprinting, interval training, and plyometric exercises like box jumps, burpees, or jump roping.

Durable materials such as Cordura, nylon, and polyester are less likely to tear from constant wear during intense movement. All of the picks on this list are made from either of these three fabrics, and I found they perform well during explosive workouts and cardio. They also wick away sweat, which is a must for ultimate comfort. As for fit, I love an adjustable closure system with a zipper or buckles at the front, waist, and shoulders for customizing the fit.

Industry observers note that since 2020, we’ve updated this story and tested every major weighted vest on the market. I’m a certified personal trainer with the National Strength and Conditioning Association. I’ve worked in the health and fitness industry for nine years and have six years of hands-on experience working with clients one-on-one and in small group settings. With experience testing and reviewing hundreds of fitness products over the years, I wore select weighted vests for multiple hour-long walks and workouts, including exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, lunges, planks, and box jumps. I paid close attention to the material to see how it held up against sweat, fit for comfort, and weight for resistance levels. I also kept notes of my likes and dislikes.

WH editors, including associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, art director Christine Giordano, and contributor Korin Miller, also tested a few options and provided extensive notes on their experiences with them. Read on for our thoughts on the best weighted vests for women, as well as some other recommendations we like but haven't tested personally.

Lauren Strong is a NSCA-Certified Personal Trainer who has worked in the health and fitness industry for almost a decade. She coaches clients on the fundamentals of dumbbell and barbell training in one-on-one and group settings. Jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, is the executive health and fitness director at Women’s Health, where she oversees all health and fitness content across WomensHealthMag.com and the print magazine. Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

According to recent reports, surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

According to recent reports, after Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 blueprint, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

In a recent development, so Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

In a recent development, besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

In a recent development, you can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.
